text.p: Ian Strachan, who is piloting Anglo-Australian diversified industrials group BTR through a huge divestment and restructuring plan, said on Wednesday that he intended the transition to create value for shareholders. The chief executive, who took over at the start of this year, said that the key point of the restructuring was the prospects for the units idenitified as core for the future.

"The retained group with (1995-equivalent) sales of 7.0 billion stg has a return on capital after adding back goodwill of 16.4 percent. This is significantly value-creating as far as shareholders are concerned," he told Reuters in an interview.

Including the 182.5 million stg sale of its electric power group, provisionally agreed on Thursday, BTR has completed about two-thirds of its planned divestments and has a range of smaller units with sales equal to about 840 million stg left to sell.
The biggest tranche of disposals, including its Taiwanese polymer interests, the U.S. assets of aggregates group Tilcon and the electric power units, has been done in the past 10 days.

Thursday's half-year results carried two big exceptional provisions: one of 273 million stg, covering anticipated losses on forthcoming sales, and another of 349 million stg, putting aside costs of closures and restructuring in the retained group.
Strachan said these restructuring items, some 45 percent of which will be used in continental Europe, had been planned in detail and would be stuck to rigorously.
"I think it's very difficult in continental Europe to drive through restructuring, but we intend to do that," he said.
"The point I'd like to emphasise about this restructuring is it's a programme -- it's very specific (and) it's one off. It is clearly part of our strategy of growth going forward."
Within the restructuring provision, 225 million stg will go on internal reorganisation, of which 187 million in cash costs, and 124 million will pay for closures, 102 million in cash.

Part of the documentation provided alongside the interim results was a proforma statement of how the results of BTR's continuing operations looked, before taking into account all the exceptional provisions.
On sales of 4.49 billion stg at the half-year, up from a proforma 3.96 billion stg in the same 1995 period, profit before tax and interest rose to 703 millon stg from 684 million stg.

Total earnings per share slipped to 10.7 pence from 12.5 pence -- a reflection of some trading pressure in the automotive systems areas, above all -- while pretax profit would have been 626 million stg versus 729 million stg in the year-ago period.

Finance director Kathleen O'Donovan said the rest of the continuing group, other than automotive, was growing and that the 1995 year-end return on capital calculation of 16.4 percent remained a fair guide of current performance.
Beyond seeking to exit those areas which have been a drag on the business, Strachan said it was important for BTR to seek market leadership from its key future "building block" units.

"The target is not described necessarily in mathematical terms. (It) is to achieve a position in these major global groups as an undisputed leader, (which) means having substantial market share and distinctive competitive advantages."
Already, Strachan noted, many of the BTR units in areas like process valves, power drives and industrial batteries lead their competitors in market, technology, product or cost terms.
"These are very strong market positions. We're not talking about aspirations that are not found in reality. This is today."

Tactics for the future would include the continued search for bolt-on acquisitions for the growth groups, as well as an ambition to focus heavily on emerging markets -- in the hope that by 2000, 15 percent of group sales would be from such areas where it sees high growth and manufacturing opportunities.
